vt.analysis:
Type: OpenClaw Skill
Name: self-updater
Version: 1.4.1

The skill bundle describes a self-updater that performs high-risk system operations, including updating the OpenClaw core, modifying installed skills, and restarting the gateway service. It requires reading sensitive configuration files (~/.openclaw/openclaw.json) and scheduled task data, and it explicitly instructs the use of ExecutionPolicy Bypass for its PowerShell scripts (scripts/self-updater.ps1). While these actions are consistent with the stated purpose of a maintenance tool, the combination of broad file access, service control, and the ability to execute remote code via updates represents a significant attack surface.

llm.summary: The skill's description (auto-update, cron-aware, idle detection) is plausible, but the runtime instructions reference missing scripts and local config files, and the package declares no credentials or install steps—these inconsistencies raise concerns about what code will actually run and what secrets it may read or use.

dimensions.detail: The stated purpose (auto-update OpenClaw core & skills, respect cron/idle, notify channels) aligns with reading OpenClaw config and restarting the gateway. However the registry metadata lists no required binaries or env vars while SKILL.md explicitly requires PowerShell, npm, clawhub CLI, and Windows—an internal mismatch. The README/SKILL.md claim an open-source GitHub repo but the skill metadata provides no homepage/source URL.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: SKILL.md instructs running scripts/scripts/self-updater.ps1 and reading ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json and ~/.openclaw/cron/jobs.json. No code files are packaged with the skill, so the actual updater logic would come from an external script (git clone, ClawHub install, or remote repo). The instructions therefore grant the updater potential to read local config (which may contain tokens), update core/skills, and restart services — but the exact commands and network endpoints are not present to audit.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: There is no install spec in the registry bundle (instruction-only). README suggests installing via ClawHub or git clone from GitHub—pulling and running code from an external repository is needed to realize the skill. That external fetch is not included in the packaged skill and so cannot be audited here; fetching/executing remote scripts is a supply-chain risk.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The skill declares no required env vars or credentials but states it will auto-detect/send notifications via Telegram/Feishu and will read ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json. That file could contain gateway credentials or channel tokens. The absence of declared credential requirements is inconsistent and means sensitive data could be read/used without explicit permission documentation.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The skill does not request 'always:true', and is user-invocable, but its intended actions (updating core/skills, restarting the gateway) are privileged operations on the host and on other skills. Because no code is bundled here, it is unclear what safety checks actually run; autonomous invocation combined with privileged actions increases risk if the external script is malicious or tampered with.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance: This skill is plausible for performing safe auto-updates, but there are important red flags you should address before installing or running it: (1) The package contains no updater script—SKILL.md references scripts/self-updater.ps1 that are not packaged here. Inspect the referenced GitHub repo (scripts/self-updater.ps1) before running anything. (2) Confirm where updates are downloaded from and verify signatures/hashes. (3) Check ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json and cron file contents to understand what secrets (gateway tokens, channel webhooks) the updater could read; ensure sensitive tokens are stored and scoped appropriately. (4) Do a manual dry-run in a sandbox or test instance first (no AutoApprove, NoNotify) and preserve backups. (5) Prefer installing from a known repository URL and review the PowerShell script for network calls, data exfiltration, and restart commands. If you cannot review the external scripts or the GitHub source, treat this skill as high-risk and avoid enabling automatic/unsupervised updates.
